subject: Accounting
title: Life-Cycle Costing
description: A quick, practical guide to Life-Cycle Costing.

hook.text: A cheap printer costs $50. But ink cartridges over its life cost $500. Which is the real cost?

buildup.text: Life-cycle costing captures all costs from design through disposal—not just the purchase price.

discovery.text: It includes R&D, production, marketing, warranty, maintenance, and end-of-life disposal.

twist.text: Products that look cheap at launch can be wildly expensive over their full life cycle.

climax.text: Smart buyers and smart managers evaluate total cost of ownership, not sticker price.

punchline.text: The purchase price is just the first installment.

quiz.question: What does life-cycle costing include?
options: All costs from design through disposal

details.summary: Life-cycle costing tracks all costs associated with a product from conception through disposal—including R&D, design, production, distribution, customer service, and end-of-life costs. This topic explains why looking at the full cost picture matters for strategic pricing.
details.whyItMatters: Most products incur significant costs before and after the production phase. Pricing based only on manufacturing costs can lead to products that never recover their full lifecycle investment.
takeaways: Up to 80-90% of a product's total lifecycle costs are committed during the design phase
Warranty, support, and disposal costs can be substantial and are often underestimated
Life-cycle costing enables better go/no-go decisions and more accurate long-term profitability analysis

faq.question: What is life-cycle costing?
faq.answer: Life-cycle costing captures all costs over a product's entire life—from research and development through design, manufacturing, marketing, distribution, customer support, warranty, and disposal. It provides the complete cost picture for evaluating true product profitability.

faq.question: Why are most costs committed during the design phase?
faq.answer: Design decisions determine materials, manufacturing complexity, labor requirements, serviceability, and durability. Once a product is designed, 80-90% of its eventual costs are locked in. This is why cost management is most impactful during early design stages.
